title: It Is Raining Fish: The Mysterious Phenomenon of Animal Rain

segments.text_content: On a June morning in 2010, residents of the remote Australian town of Lajamanu stepped outside to find their streets covered in small, wriggling fish. Hundreds of spangled perch were falling from a cloudless sky, landing alive and flopping on roads, rooftops, and lawns. The nearest body of water was over 300 kilometres away. It was not the first time this had happened in Lajamanu -- and it would not be the last. The skies over our planet occasionally rain animals, and the phenomenon is far better documented than most people realize.

segments.text_content: Records of animal rain stretch back thousands of years. The Bible describes a plague of frogs descending on Egypt. The Roman author Pliny the Elder documented storms of frogs and fish in first-century writings. In 1794, French soldiers stationed in Lalain reported a downpour of toads during a rainstorm. For centuries, these reports were dismissed as superstition or exaggeration. But in the twentieth century, as meteorological science advanced, the mechanism behind animal rain was finally understood -- and it turned out to be impressively mundane.

segments.text_content: The engine of animal rain is the waterspout -- a tornado that forms over open water. When the rotating column of air touches down on a shallow lake, pond, or flooded field, it creates an enormous suction effect at its base. Water, sediment, and any organisms near the surface are vacuumed upward into the column with tremendous force. Small, light animals -- frogs, small fish, tiny crabs, earthworms -- can be lifted hundreds of meters into the atmosphere in seconds, often alive and unharmed by the initial ascent.

segments.text_content: Once lofted into the upper atmosphere, animals can be transported enormous distances. Jet stream winds and the upper currents associated with storm systems can carry a payload of frogs or fish for tens to hundreds of kilometres before the storm loses energy or the animals are deposited by rainfall. This explains why the fish that fell on Lajamanu were identified as spangled perch -- a species native to the Kimberley and Northern Territory rivers, hundreds of kilometres to the north, in the direction of prevailing storm tracks.

segments.text_content: Most remarkable of all, many animals survive the entire ordeal. At altitude, temperatures can plunge well below freezing. Small frogs and fish have been found frozen solid within hailstones -- essentially cryopreserved mid-flight. As they descend and temperatures rise, they thaw, revive, and resume normal activity. Witnesses to frog rain events consistently report that the animals are alive and hopping when they land. The creatures are, in effect, involuntary passengers on a meteorological roller coaster that ends with them deposited alive, hundreds of kilometres from home.

segments.text_content: In 2009, the town of Rakow in Germany experienced one of the more dramatic recorded animal rain events when hundreds of earthworms fell during a storm, covering roads and gardens. In 2012, residents of Chitral in northern Pakistan reported a rain of small fish during a thunderstorm. In 2017, a rain of small octopuses was reported in a coastal town in China during a cyclone. The range of animals documented falling from the sky is extraordinary: shrimp, crabs, snakes, spiders, beetles, and even -- in at least one nineteenth-century account -- small alligators in South Carolina.

segments.text_content: The meteorological conditions required for animal rain are specific but not rare. Waterspouts form most readily in warm, humid coastal and lacustrine environments during convective storm season. The Gulf Coast of the United States, the Mediterranean, the coastlines of Australia, and the shallow lakes of sub-Saharan Africa are particularly prone to the waterspouts capable of lifting biological material. In some regions, local ecologies have adapted -- small fish populations that inhabit isolated lakes may have been periodically seeded there by animal rain events.

segments.text_content: Scientists now accept animal rain as a fully documented, physically explicable natural phenomenon. In 2000, the Royal Meteorological Society of the United Kingdom published a formal assessment concluding that the evidence for waterspout-mediated animal rain was sound. The phenomenon has been captured on video multiple times. Weather radar data has provided corroborating evidence in several modern cases, showing biological echo signatures -- a phenomenon meteorologists call angel echo -- tracking from waterspout events to subsequent animal fall locations.

segments.text_content: There is an ironic ecological dimension to animal rain. For isolated water bodies -- desert ponds, volcanic island lakes, landlocked pools -- animal rain may actually be a mechanism of ecological seeding. Fish and frog species have been found in bodies of water with no apparent natural connection to other water sources. Genetic analysis of some isolated populations suggests colonization events consistent with single, small founder groups arriving simultaneously -- exactly what a waterspout deposit would produce. The sky is, occasionally, a dispersal mechanism.

segments.text_content: The next time rain darkens the air and thunder rolls across the horizon, it is worth pausing over the strangeness of what might be riding those storm currents. The atmosphere -- that thin, restless shell of gas wrapping our planet -- is not merely moving air and water. It is, on occasion, a living conveyor, carrying the small and the helpless across distances they could never traverse on their own. Nature finds ways. Sometimes, quite literally, it drops them from the sky.
